title: Power supplies and regulators
blurb: Explain how linear and switching regulators hold voltage steady, read Figure E7-2, and calculate battery time and regulator heat.

E7D01.why: A linear regulator **varies the conduction of a control element** (pass transistor) to hold the output voltage constant.
E7D01.trap: Duty-cycle control is a switching regulator; linear ones always keep the pass transistor.

E7D02.why: A switchmode regulator turns the input on and off and **varies the duty cycle of the pulses going into a filter**.
E7D02.trap: Varying a pass element's conductivity is linear regulation.

E7D03.why: A **Zener diode** holds a nearly fixed voltage when reverse biased, so it makes a stable reference.
E7D03.trap: An SCR is a latching switch; converters change signal form, not hold a reference.

E7D04.why: A three-terminal regulator passes the load current **in series** with the output: a **series regulator**.
E7D04.trap: Shunt and current-source choices don't describe the in-line pass element.

E7D05.why: A **shunt regulator** sits across the output and so loads the unregulated source, with a series resistor dropping the excess.
E7D05.trap: A series regulator sits in the path; it does not load the source in the same way.

E7D06.why: Q1 is the pass transistor: it **controls the current** so the output voltage stays constant.
E7D06.trap: It does not chop the input; there is no switching in this circuit.

E7D07.why: C2 across the Zener **bypasses rectifier ripple around D1**, keeping the reference steady.
E7D07.trap: It isn't an output filter, and it doesn't provide the bias; D1 and R1 do.

E7D08.why: A pass transistor is varied to hold the output: a **linear voltage regulator**.
E7D08.trap: Common emitter and common base are amplifier stages; here the output tracks the Zener.

E7D09.why: Time = capacity ÷ current. Example: 60 Ah ÷ 5 A = **12 hours**.
E7D09.trap: Dividing current by capacity inverts the answer: more capacity must give more time.

E7D10.why: High switching frequency allows **much smaller transformers and filter parts** for the same output power.
E7D10.trap: Switching supplies still need output filters; they are just smaller.

E7D11.why: Panels give DC. An **inverter converts DC to AC**.
E7D11.trap: Ripple reduction, voltage control and blocking reverse discharge are other parts' jobs.

E7D12.why: Dropout is the **minimum input-to-output voltage** a linear regulator needs to keep regulating.
E7D12.trap: It's not a maximum drop or a power rating; it's a minimum headroom.

E7D13.why: The pass element burns the voltage it drops: **(Vin − Vout) × Iout**. Example: (25 − 12) × 2 = 26 W.
E7D13.trap: Vout × Iout is the load's power; Vin × Iin is the total taken from the supply.

E7D14.why: Equal resistors across series capacitors **equalize voltage, discharge them, and provide a minimum load**: all three.

E7D15.why: A step-start limits inrush so the **filter capacitors charge gradually**. Empty capacitors look like a short at turn-on.
E7D15.trap: It doesn't change voltage or compensate for line variations.
